domain: control-theory and capacity-planning economics for orchestration gates (isolation-mode crossover, controller build/defer, pre-spawn check cost)
axioms: A dynamic controller must be justified by a measured signal before it is written — building it against an assumed-but-unmeasured conflict rate is premature optimization

Every policy gate (crossover width, conflict-rate threshold, N-tasks check gate) must be expressed as an explicit, falsifiable threshold with a named input signal, not left as an implicit or prose-only rule
A safety/pre-spawn check has its own cost, and that cost must be weighed against the cost of the failure it prevents — a check can become the bottleneck it exists to avoid

Two cost curves are only commensurable on a single crossover axis if they are actually the same shape (one-time setup cost vs continuous contention cost are not automatically comparable) — assuming a crossover exists is itself a claim requiring proof

A measurement regime that only observes outcomes already suppressed by the mechanism under evaluation cannot produce the signal needed to justify replacing that mechanism (interlock suppressing conflicts near-zero cannot itself generate evidence that a controller is unneeded, only evidence that interlock works under current load)

Sequential decision gates (cost gate, pre-spawn conflict check, hypothetical controller) compound in cost and failure probability — evaluating them as independent checks undercounts real risk and real overhead
primitives: isolation mode (per-repo worktree vs interlock-coordinated shared tree) and its cost shape (one-time setup vs continuous contention)
crossover width (fan-out size at which one isolation mode's total cost exceeds the other's)
conflict rate / near-miss rate (measured signal gating the controller decision)
gate cost (wall-clock cost of evaluating a pre-spawn check, scaling with fan-out width N)
falsifiability criterion (a stated N-conflicts-in-M-fan-outs-over-window condition that would flip a build/defer decision)
measurement bias (a suppression mechanism whose success prevents the very signal that would justify replacing it)
failure_mode: Treats every threshold as a math problem to be solved from first principles, potentially under-weighting organizational/governance reasons a gate might need an owner and review cadence rather than just a better formula

Can be too skeptical of building a controller (correctly diagnosing the measurement-bias trap) without offering an alternative instrumentation design that resolves it, leaving the objection unconstructive if not paired with a concrete near-miss-tracking proposal

Less equipped to judge whether Rimsky-vs-Mycroft-vs-lbkd is the right set of layers at all — takes the existence of Rimsky's gates as given and reasons only about their internal calibration, potentially missing that a different orchestrator topology would eliminate the need for a given gate entirely
